chunks: Muhammad ibn al-Qasim narrated from Safwan ibn Yahya from Muawiya ibn Ammar, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a tree whose root is in the Haram (sanctuary) and its branch is in the Hal (permissible area). He said, 'Its branch is prohibited because of the location of its root.' I said, 'What if its root is in the Hal and its branch is in the Haram?' He said, 'Its root is prohibited because of the location of its branch.' And everything that grows in the Haram, it is not permissible to uproot it in any way.

key_terms.الْحَرَمِ: Sanctuary (specifically Mecca or Medina, where specific rules apply)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on a tree whose root is in the Haram and branch in the Hal?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the principle of *ta'alluq* (connection) in Islamic jurisprudence, where the status of the root or branch determines the permissibility of the entire tree for the pilgrim. It highlights the strict sanctity of the Haram boundaries, ensuring that no part of the vegetation is removed in a way that violates the sacred status of the area, whether the origin lies within or outside the sanctuary. This ruling is crucial for understanding the practical application of *kaffarah* (expiation) for pilgrims who inadvertently harvest trees crossing these boundaries.
